children: 0756 GMT - Eurozone government bond yields rise in opening trade, tracking U.S. Treasury yields higher, as oil prices rebound slightly from Monday's slide. With no key economic data in the eurozone, and government bond auctions only from Austria and Germany, investors' focus is the U.S. midterm elections. Odds of a Democratic sweep have increased. "Democratic control of Congress should, on balance, be Treasury positive," says Commerzbank's Christoph Rieger in a note. "Predicting the election outcome is one thing; anticipating Donald Trump's and the market's reaction is another," he says. The 10-year German Bund yield rises 2.1 basis points to 3.316%. Belgium's 10-year OLO is among underperformers with its yield up 3.2 basis points at 4.428% following the collapse of budget talks. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0747 GMT - The U.S. midterms are a key test for oil prices as investors parse the outcome for the administration's next move in the Middle East, the duration of supply disruptions and crude's geopolitical premium, says Ipek Ozkardeskaya at Swissquote. If Democrats gain control of one or both chambers, they could increase scrutiny of war policy, challenge military funding and increase pressure for a diplomatic solution once the new Congress is formed. "Markets, however, could anticipate that pressure immediately," she says. And if that's followed by credible negotiations and prospects of safer shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, oil prices could fall sustainably. However, a weaker Republican position wouldn't automatically mean a lower geopolitical risk premium, even if it adds pressure for a diplomatic resolution. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0744 GMT - The Chinese central bank's move to raise the foreign-exchange reserve requirement ratio for financial institutions is aimed at slowing down, not reversing, the yuan's appreciation trend, Standard Chartered's Becky Liu says in a note. The measure won't be sufficient to alter fundamental flows--such as exporter foreign-exchange conversion or cross-border investments, but it should be useful to reduce speculative positioning, the head of greater China strategy says. Its direct impact is small, but the signaling effect is more important, Liu says. The PBOC's move indicates that the recent pace of the yuan's appreciation is considered too rapid, she says. StanChart continues to expect the dollar at around 6.65 yuan at end-2026. The dollar is at 6.6711 yuan in onshore trading. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)

0739 GMT - The dollar falls on AI concerns and investor jitters ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections. Apple on Monday warned that the cost of serving its AI tools would squeeze its margins, fuelling worries about the sustainability of AI investments. AI model maker Anthropic posted an operating loss for the third quarter due to a pricey data-center deal while rival OpenAI raised less than half of the $30 billion it had initially targeted for its latest funding round. More positively for the dollar, oil prices turn higher after the U.S. attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday. However, uncertainty over the midterms keeps investors cautious. The DXY dollar index falls 0.1% to 101.684, having reached a one-month low of 101.426 Monday. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0729 GMT - China is unlikely to roll out large-scale policy support despite weak factory activity data in October, according to BofA Securities in a research note. China's official purchasing managers' index fell into contraction territory last month and missed market expectations, the bank points out. However, BofA continues to believe that "policymakers are unlikely to pivot decisively toward supporting domestic demand unless export growth slows meaningfully". The coming October trade data will be key to assessing whether the deterioration in purchasing managers' index export orders signals a broader slowdown in exports, the bank says. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0641 GMT - Thailand's headline consumer-price index likely rose 3.5% on year in October, up from September's 2.82% increase, according to the median forecast from a Wall Street Journal poll of seven economists. Prices likely rose due to higher energy costs and a rebound in food inflation, DBS economists say in a report. The Bank of Thailand said at its last meeting in October that it expects a temporary rise in inflation this year. The CPI data are due this week. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0632 GMT - The Federal Reserve should back off its "irrational rate increase policy" as monetary policy should focus on core inflation and not inflation driven by oil prices, says Jay Hatfield at Infrastructure Capital Advisors. The Fed should recognize its primary impact is on the interest-sensitive sectors of the economy which is dominated by housing, says the CEO and portfolio manager. Hatfield urges fundamental reform of the Fed's forecasting models, the arbitrary 2% inflation target, and the "deeply flawed inflation indices it follows." Infrastructure Capital Advisors is also looking forward to the Fed's task force results that may address some of these fundamental flaws, he says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0615 GMT - A combination of softer labor market data, evidence of slowing consumer demand or additional tightening in financial conditions could reduce the odds of an interest-rate hike by the Federal Reserve in December, says JoAnne Bianco at BondBloxx Investment Management in a note. "A broader pattern of moderating growth and easing inflation pressures would likely make the Fed more comfortable remaining on hold," the senior investment strategist says. Markets have shown that rate hike expectations can move quickly when incoming data challenge the narrative of a resilient economy, she adds. Money markets currently price a 74% probability of a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike in December, according to LSEG. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0610 GMT - ​This difficult environment for bonds is likely to persist for a while but yield levels are too high, Mediolanum International Funds Limited's Daniel Loughney says in a note. "We expect monetary authorities to adopt a less hawkish stance to reduce the degree of financial tightening priced into markets, which would pull longer-dated yields lower," the head of fixed income says. This leaves Mediolanum constructive on government debt at current elevated yield levels, he says. The outlook for credit, meanwhile, will depend on whether monetary authorities react too slowly, he says. "The longer higher yields persist, the more stress credit sectors will feel." (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0547 GMT - Inflation in the Philippines likely hit multiyear highs in October, according to the median forecast from a Wall Street Journal poll of eight economists. They expect headline CPI to have risen 7.9% on year, the highest reading since February 2023. Crude oil prices surged to six-month highs by end-October, which will keep domestic fuel prices at elevated levels, ANZ Research's Kausani Basak says in a report. Food prices also likely picked up as rice costs rose, the FX analyst says. The CPI data are due on Thursday.(amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0546 GMT - Consumer inflation in South Korea could gradually return to the central bank's 2% target through 2027--earlier than the bank expects, says Nomura's Jeong Woo Park. Weaker consumption and a softer housing market could ease the Bank of Korea's concerns about price and financial stability, while the semiconductor boom has had a limited impact, the economist says. Headline inflation, which eased to 2.8% in October from 2.9% in the previous month, provides limited evidence of renewed inflation pressures, as declines in agricultural prices offset increases in industrial goods and services, he says. Nomura continues to expect the BOK to raise interest rates by 25 basis points each in November and February, citing "elevated and sticky" core inflation. (kwanwoo.jun@wsj.com)

0529 GMT - RBA Gov. Michele Bullock has delivered an evenhanded press conference, giving little away on the outlook for interest rates. Still, she did say that inflation expectations remain skewed to the upside and that the bank will do what is needed to get inflation down. The RBA revised up its forecasts for inflation in the years ahead and a return to target is now further away than it was at the start of the year. Nevertheless, the interest rate cycle does feel more mature now, so the peak in rates can't be far away. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)
